title: National multi-city demonstrations demanding Alexei Navalny’s release
location: Multiple cities across Russia, including Moscow and St Petersburg; national reporting also names other regions. Interfax documents a Jan. 23 gathering in Khabarovsk.
scope: National coordinated multi-city action; local gatherings are not split automatically. In Khabarovsk, reporting describes one physical action with both Navalny- and Furgal-support demands; it is not duplicated as a second local event.
organizer: Navalny’s allies/backers called for demonstrations; local organizers may have varied.
participants_original: For central Moscow, The Moscow Times reports an Interior Ministry estimate around 4,000 and media estimates from 15,000 to 40,000; DW reports a 15,000–50,000 range. These site-specific estimates differ and are not summed into a national total. In Khabarovsk, one Jan. 23 gathering supporting both Navalny and Furgal drew about 250 by the city administration’s estimate and 200–300 by DVhab’s estimate, as reported by Interfax; these are not summed.
threshold_50_evidence: The threshold is supported at the same named site: central Moscow reports range from an Interior Ministry estimate around 4,000 to media estimates of 15,000–40,000 in The Moscow Times and 15,000–50,000 in DW. Even the lowest reported site estimate exceeds 50; the national total remains unbounded. Interfax also reports a same-site Khabarovsk estimate of about 250 from the city administration and 200–300 from DVhab for the single Jan. 23 action.

title.summary: Both contemporaneous reports describe 23 January demonstrations across Russia; this is a working national-wave label pending episode review.

start_date.summary: The Moscow Times dates the report Jan. 23, 2021; The Guardian dates its report Saturday 23 Jan 2021. DW metadata also says 23 Jan, although one body sentence says February; that conflict is recorded separately.

end_date.summary: The accessed sections do not establish a national physical end or complete dissolution. No end date is assigned from article publication or a local report. For Khabarovsk, Interfax relays a 14:48 local report that the gathering had nearly subsided; it does not establish complete departure or a national end.

location.summary: The Moscow Times reports over 100 towns and cities; Guardian names Moscow, St Petersburg, Vladivostok and Yakutsk. The list is not a complete site inventory. Interfax also names Khabarovsk.

scope.summary: Reports describe a nationwide call and actions across many cities. Physical local episodes and site-level boundaries remain open for review. In Khabarovsk, Interfax describes a single action supporting both Navalny and Furgal, linking the local Furgal campaign to the Jan. 23 Navalny call without splitting the same gathering.

organizer.summary: The Moscow Times attributes the call to Navalny backers; Guardian refers to Navalny allies and supporters. This does not identify every local organizer.

demands.summary: The reports describe demands for Navalny’s release and against the arrest/state corruption; this is directed at Russian state conduct. HRW identifies these demands explicitly. Interfax reports that Khabarovsk participants also voiced support for Furgal and describes the older Saturday demand to free him.

participants_original.summary: Moscow estimates differ: Interior Ministry around 4,000; media 15,000–40,000 in The Moscow Times; DW 15,000–50,000. HRW also reports several thousand in named Siberian cities and around 300 in Yakutsk. No sites are summed. For Khabarovsk, Interfax attributes about 250 to the municipal administration and 200–300 to DVhab; these estimates are kept separate.

threshold_50_evidence.summary: Same-site support: the reported central-Moscow estimates are all above 50 (official around 4,000; media ranges 15,000–40,000 and 15,000–50,000). HRW separately reports several thousand in Novosibirsk, Tyumen and Yekaterinburg and around 300 in Yakutsk; these locations are not summed. Interfax documents a second same-site example at Lenin Square in Khabarovsk: about 250 by the municipal account and 200–300 by DVhab for the same gathering.

protester_violence.summary: Guardian reports snowballs and physical exchanges in named sites; HRW says incidents were limited and describes snow-throwing/altercations at Yekaterinburg and an attack on a vehicle in Moscow. These are not assigned to every local gathering.

state_response.accommodation.summary: The accessed account does not document reception or negotiation with protesters; accommodation remains unknown.

state_response.arrests.summary: Contemporary reports and HRW attribute thousands of Jan. 23 detentions to police. These national totals are response evidence only, not participant counts. In Khabarovsk, Interfax reports detentions and attributes an estimate of at least ten people taken to DVhab.

state_response.beatings.summary: Guardian, DW and HRW report baton beatings and other physical force at named sites including Moscow, St Petersburg, Yekaterinburg, Orenburg and Khabarovsk. Evidence is site-specific and is not generalized to every city.

state_response.crowd_dispersal.summary: Guardian reports police driving crowds from Pushkin Square; HRW documents loudspeaker warnings, an announcement that the Moscow gathering was illegal, demands that people leave, and dispersal at named sites.

state_response.ignore.summary: The Kremlin’s delayed public reaction is not coded as ignore; no explicit refusal or avoidance of a request is established.

state_response.killings.summary: The Guardian states that no one was reported to have died at the time of publication; this is a bounded report, not independent confirmation of no deaths.

state_response.shootings.summary: HRW mentions officers carrying assault rifles in Yekaterinburg, but no report establishes firearm discharge at the event; rifles, batons and other force are not coded as shooting.

notes: National aggregate evidence supports one proposed coordinated wave. Site-specific counts, organization and response vary; national arrests are not turnout. Physical end is unknown. Distinct local actions with additional demands require review before separation or merging. HRW independently describes its own review of video, photos and reporting, with site-specific turnout and police conduct; the national wave still has incomplete city coverage. Interfax confirms one Khabarovsk Jan. 23 action included both Navalny and Furgal support, at the same site and time; it is represented within E001 rather than duplicated. The local 14:48 “nearly subsided” update is not treated as complete departure or national physical end.
open_questions: How should the unavailable Coding Procedure represent a coordinated call across multiple physical sites?
Which local actions had distinct organizers or additional state demands?
What was the physical end at each site?
Can source coverage support more complete regional turnout and response without treating national aggregate counts as site evidence?

title: National multi-city demonstrations demanding Alexei Navalny’s release
location: Multiple Russian cities from Siberia and the Far East to St Petersburg and Moscow, including a Jan. 31 central-square action in Khabarovsk reported by Mediazona and DW. Kommersant’s selected live updates also name regional sites in Krasnodar, Voronezh, Penza and Stavropol.
scope: A second coordinated national call with physical gatherings at multiple local sites; retained as one proposed national action pending unit guidance.
organizer: Navalny’s allies called for new protests; local organizers may have varied.
participants_original: At the site level, The Moscow Times reports about 7,000 in Yekaterinburg (attributed to Znak), about 5,000 in Novosibirsk (local media), and hundreds near Pionerskaya in St Petersburg. In Khabarovsk, DW later reports 70–80 at Lenin Square; Mediazona’s contemporaneous live page describes several dozen at a central square. The Khabarovsk estimates are not added together. Euronews/AP reports a dozen at a Vladivostok site. These separate figures are not summed; the national total is not bounded. Kommersant separately reports about 2,000 at the Krasnodar regional-administration square and about 300 protesters at Voronezh’s Pushkin Square, among other site reports; these estimates are not summed with the counts above.
threshold_50_evidence: The threshold is supported by same-site reports: The Moscow Times attributes approximately 7,000 in Yekaterinburg to Znak, approximately 5,000 in Novosibirsk to local media, and hundreds near Pionerskaya in St Petersburg. DW later reports 70–80 at Lenin Square in Khabarovsk, a same-site estimate above 50; Mediazona’s contemporaneous report describes several dozen in central Khabarovsk but does not itself clearly resolve the threshold. These are separate location-specific reports, not a sum. Euronews/AP separately reports a dozen in Vladivostok, which does not meet the local threshold. Kommersant’s selected live updates provide further same-site reports above 50: about 2,000 at the Krasnodar regional-administration square and about 300 protesters at Pushkin Square in Voronezh. The separate reported “about 50” in Stavropol is borderline and is not relied on for the threshold.

title.summary: Contemporary Euronews/AP and Moscow Times accounts describe the second national action on 31 January.

start_date.summary: Euronews/AP gives a publication date of 31 January and identifies the protest as Sunday, Jan. 31; the Moscow Times live blog is dated Jan. 31, 2021.

end_date.summary: Neither national report gives a complete physical end. The Moscow Times notes metro service returning to normal and reports releases from detention; neither is treated as the protest ending. DW’s account of detained people and activists leaving the Jan. 31 Khabarovsk square is site-specific and does not establish a national physical end.

location.summary: Euronews/AP names Siberia, the Far East, St Petersburg and Moscow; The Moscow Times reports detentions in more than 80 cities. Mediazona’s Jan. 31 live page places a gathering on a central square in Khabarovsk, and DW later locates a 70–80-person Jan. 31 group at Lenin Square. The site list remains incomplete. Kommersant’s selected Jan. 31 live updates also name sites in Krasnodar, Voronezh, Penza and Stavropol; the list remains incomplete.

scope.summary: The reports describe a new nationwide call by Navalny allies and multiple physical sites. Mediazona’s live chronology includes a Jan. 31 Khabarovsk central-square gathering under the national Navalny-action coverage; DW reports 70–80 in Lenin Square. Whether this Khabarovsk group also overlapped with or made Furgal-support demands remains unresolved, but it is not duplicated as an extra event.

organizer.summary: The Moscow Times says Navalny allies called for new protests; no complete roster of local organizers was reviewed.

demands.summary: The reports say the actions demanded Navalny’s release, a demand aimed at the Russian state after his detention and prospective sentence.

participants_original.summary: The Moscow Times liveblog reports about 7,000 in Yekaterinburg (Znak), about 5,000 in Novosibirsk (local media), and hundreds at named St Petersburg sites; DW reports 70–80 in Khabarovsk and Mediazona contemporaneously says several dozen at a central square. These Khabarovsk reports are not summed. Euronews/AP reports a dozen at one Vladivostok site. Kommersant separately reports about 2,000 at the Krasnodar regional-administration square and about 300 protesters at Voronezh’s Pushkin Square. These site reports are not added to one another or to the other city estimates.

threshold_50_evidence.summary: Same-site reports independently clear 50: approximately 7,000 in Yekaterinburg attributed to Znak, approximately 5,000 in Novosibirsk attributed to local media, and hundreds at named St Petersburg sites (The Moscow Times); DW later reports 70–80 at Lenin Square in Khabarovsk. Mediazona’s contemporaneous Khabarovsk description is “several dozen” and alone is not a clear threshold measure. The Vladivostok site reported by Euronews/AP was about a dozen. Kommersant separately reports about 2,000 at the Krasnodar regional-administration square and about 300 protesters at Voronezh’s Pushkin Square, each a named site above 50. Its “about 50” Stavropol report is borderline and is not relied on.

protester_violence.summary: The OVD-Info report describes some violence across the broader January–February campaign but does not date it to this event in the accessed passage; no event-specific protester violence is established.

state_response.accommodation.summary: No reception or negotiation is documented in the accessed sections; unknown.

state_response.arrests.summary: Date-specific sources and OVD-Info report detentions on Jan. 31. DW reports 13 detained among the 70–80 in Khabarovsk; Mediazona reports selective arrests and an arrested local journalist; OVD-Info’s city list records at least nine detentions there. These are response counts, not attendance. National totals differ and OVD-Info entries are same-organization evidence, not independent sources.

state_response.beatings.summary: The Moscow Times liveblog relays OVD-Info’s report of violent beatings of detained protesters in Vladivostok and reports police using electric shock batons in St Petersburg. The report is attributed and site-specific; it is not an independent inspection of footage and does not imply firearm discharge.

state_response.crowd_dispersal.summary: Euronews/AP reports riot police pushed and chased demonstrators near the Moscow prison. The Moscow Times liveblog reports police using tear gas to break up a St Petersburg group and forceful dispersal in Chelyabinsk; each claim remains tied to its reported site. Kommersant’s live correspondent reports police moved about 300 protesters from Voronezh’s Pushkin Square onto Pushkinskaya Street and describes crowds being cleared at named Moscow sites; these remain attributed, site-specific accounts.

state_response.ignore.summary: No explicit refusal or avoidance of a request is shown; silence remains unknown.

state_response.killings.summary: The accessed sections do not establish a state-caused death for this event; absence of a report is not coded as no.

state_response.shootings.summary: The Moscow Times liveblog reports an officer drawing a gun in St Petersburg, but no firearm discharge. The same liveblog’s references to tasers, stun guns and traumatic pistols also do not establish shooting.

notes: January 31 is a separate reported gathering day from January 23, linked to the same campaign but not merged. Same-site attendance estimates in Yekaterinburg, Novosibirsk and St Petersburg each clear 50; the separate Vladivostok site report says about a dozen. National detention totals differ by source and are not turnout. State beatings are reported for detained protesters in Vladivostok, attributed to OVD-Info. Physical end remains unknown. Mediazona’s contemporaneous Jan. 31 live page includes a central-square action in Khabarovsk (“several dozen”); DW later reports 70–80 at Lenin Square with 13 arrests. They are recorded as a Khabarovsk site within E002’s Jan. 31 national Navalny action, not as an additional event. Whether this local group also overlapped with the older Furgal-support sequence remains open; local arrest totals are not used as turnout. Selected Kommersant live updates add named Krasnodar and Voronezh estimates above 50 and site-specific dispersal reporting; they strengthen geographic coverage but are not summed into a national turnout.
open_questions: Does the additional Coding Procedure distinguish each national action day or campaign?
Which local sites have independently reportable gathering sizes and state responses?
What was the physical end of the national action at each site?
Can detention-count differences be reconciled without changing the yes/no response coding?
Do any later site reports establish physical departure/dissolution, beyond transport resuming or detainees being released?
Did the Khabarovsk Jan. 31 national-action crowd also make a distinct Furgal-support demand or form a separate local action?

title: Gathering at Vnukovo airport to welcome Alexei Navalny
scope: One airport arrival gathering, described primarily as supporters welcoming a returning politician.
organizer: Navalny supporters and allies; contemporary reporting says they and Navalny called for people to come to the airport.
participants_original: Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reports approximately 2,000 people came to Vnukovo to greet Navalny, citing White Counter. Fontanka observed around 200 people by a gray barrier at 17:46, including people who said they were there for different arrivals. These are different source scopes/times and are not reconciled.
threshold_50_evidence: Two same-airport estimates exceed 50: RFE/RL reports about 2,000 people came to greet Navalny; Fontanka reports around 200 by a specific barrier at 17:46. Fontanka notes the crowd included people waiting for a different celebrity, so the supporter-only attendance remains uncertain.

title.summary: Contemporary reports describe people gathering at Vnukovo on 17 January to meet/welcome Navalny.

start_date.summary: Both reports are dated 17 January 2021 and describe the same-day airport gathering.

end_date.summary: The reports do not establish a complete physical end of the airport gathering; no end date is inferred.

location.summary: All three reports identify Vnukovo airport; RFE/RL distinguishes this airport from Navalny’s eventual landing at Sheremetyevo.

scope.summary: The reported activity was an airport welcome/arrival gathering. Fontanka notes some people at the barrier expected a different celebrity.

organizer.summary: RFE/RL reports that Navalny and his allies urged people to come to the airport.

demands.summary: The opened accounts describe people waiting to welcome Navalny and contest whether greeting a passenger constituted a mass event; they do not document a demand directed at the Russian state or its policy. The state-target criterion remains unresolved.

participants_original.summary: RFE/RL cites an estimate of about 2,000 arrivals to greet Navalny; Fontanka describes around 200 by a particular barrier/time with some people reportedly waiting for another celebrity. No exact supporter-only total is derived.

threshold_50_evidence.summary: The two same-airport estimates are both above 50, but the crowd composition and observation scopes differ; attendance is enough to retain the lead, not to establish a state-directed protest.

protester_violence.summary: No specific violence by people waiting at the airport is established in the opened sections; unknown.

state_response.accommodation.summary: No reception/negotiation with a state-directed demand is documented; unknown.

state_response.arrests.summary: Meduza reports an OVD-Info tally at a time on Jan. 17; RFE/RL reports over 50 detained at Vnukovo. These are state arrests, not attendance.

state_response.beatings.summary: Meduza relays reports that some people were dragged along the pavement during detention, but this does not independently establish beatings; unknown.

state_response.crowd_dispersal.summary: Meduza reports OMON used loudspeakers to tell non-passengers to leave and pushed people outside; RFE/RL reports OMON moved the welcoming crowd into the street.

state_response.ignore.summary: No explicit refusal/avoidance of a request is established; unknown.

state_response.killings.summary: The opened reports do not establish a death in this airport gathering; no negative is inferred from silence.

state_response.shootings.summary: No firearm shooting is reported in the opened airport coverage; field remains unknown.

notes: This is a high-attendance lead with an unclear state target. Do not code a political welcome as a protest demand. The Vnukovo gathering is distinct from Navalny’s landing at Sheremetyevo and from nine single pickets reported at Gostiny Dvor in St Petersburg.
open_questions: Did attendees at Vnukovo make an explicit demand to the Russian government or its policy, beyond welcoming Navalny?
How many attendees were Navalny supporters versus people waiting for other arrivals?
What attendance and demand evidence exists for the separate St Petersburg pickets at Gostiny Dvor?

title: Saturday rally in support of Sergey Furgal at Lenin Square
scope: Local Saturday rally within the longer Khabarovsk Furgal-support campaign; whether it is an independently coded episode or continuation is unresolved.
organizer: Not identified in the accessed January report.
participants_original: More than 100, by eyewitness estimates as reported by MK Khabarovsk.
threshold_50_evidence: The January report describes more than 100 people at the same named site, Lenin Square, by eyewitness estimates. This qualitative attributed estimate clears the 50-person threshold; it is not a precise count.

title.summary: MK Khabarovsk describes a traditional Saturday rally supporting Sergey Furgal.

start_date.summary: The body/page context dates the physical Saturday rally to Jan. 9, 2021. The source also describes a weekly campaign begun after Furgal’s 2020 arrest, so this date is the observed gathering date, while the episode-level onset/ownership remains pending review.

end_date.summary: MK says the Jan. 9 action lasted briefly, but gives no exact time or clear physical departure/dissolution. Its duration language is retained; the end date remains unknown.

location.summary: MK Khabarovsk locates the Jan. 9 rally at Lenin Square in Khabarovsk.

scope.summary: The January article calls this a traditional Saturday action; July 2020 contemporaneous reports establish earlier Furgal-support rallies. They do not show uninterrupted physical occupation or settle episode boundaries.

organizer.summary: The accessed January report does not identify an organizer.

demands.summary: The article identifies a Furgal-support rally and a 'Free Furgal' demand/slogan, directed at the Russian authorities holding him. The category is political_behavior_process; earlier July reports further document state-directed demands but are not used as Jan. 9 attendance evidence.

participants_original.summary: The report attributes an estimate of more than 100 people to eyewitnesses. No precise count or upper bound is given.

threshold_50_evidence.summary: An eyewitness estimate of more than 100 attendees at Lenin Square clears 50 at this site, though the estimate is qualitative and attributed.

protester_violence.summary: The accessed report does not establish event-specific protester violence; code unknown rather than infer absence.

state_response.accommodation.summary: The report does not describe receipt or negotiation of demands; response unknown.

state_response.arrests.summary: The report does not establish arrests at this gathering; response unknown.

state_response.beatings.summary: The report does not establish state beatings at this gathering; response unknown.

state_response.crowd_dispersal.summary: The report does not establish an attempt to clear this gathering; response unknown.

state_response.ignore.summary: The report does not establish explicit official avoidance/refusal of a request; response unknown.

state_response.killings.summary: The report does not establish any death in response to this gathering; response unknown.

state_response.shootings.summary: The report does not establish firearm discharge in response to this gathering; response unknown.

notes: MK’s Jan. 9 headline/body date and its 'traditional Saturday rally' description support a physical gathering that day; its photo caption instead says 'today, 9 December,' a source-internal date conflict. The same report says weekly rallies began after Furgal’s July 2020 arrest. E004 preserves the January gathering but does not decide whether it is a separate event or an older-onset unit. July attendance is not transferred to January. The report says the action lasted briefly, but gives no precise end time or departure account. Jan. 2 reports are conflicting leads only: one search-result title and partial NEWSru page suggest several dozen attendees despite a municipal cessation statement; the NEWSru body was not reviewed and the Vedomosti URL returned 404.
open_questions: Does the unit protocol treat recurring Saturday rallies as separate events or as one campaign/episode, and what interruption evidence sets the boundary?
Do Jan. 2 reports establish a qualifying gathering, a cessation claim, or a different physical sequence?
Can the Jan. 9 caption’s December reference be resolved from an archived/versioned page?
What state responses occurred at the Jan. 9 gathering?
Do the Jan. 2 claims identify a separate qualifying gathering or a small continuation? Body access and turnout remain unresolved.

participants_original: No attendance estimate available in the accessible search result.
threshold_50_evidence: Unknown. The accessible result title says another protest occurred but does not provide turnout; the article body returned HTTP 403.

title: Furgal-support gathering and detentions reported at Khabarovsk’s Lenin Square
location: Lenin Square / the square before the regional administration, Khabarovsk, Russia
scope: A Jan. 30 local Furgal-support action is described differently by two reports: RFE/RL says several dozen attended a rally, while DW says police prevented people from gathering together and detained several people walking across the square. Physical extent and relation to the weekly series remain unresolved.
participants_original: RFE/RL reports “several dozen” at a Furgal-support rally. DW reports that on Jan. 30 police prevented people from gathering together, detained several people walking across Lenin Square, and others left after seeing no group assembled. The accounts conflict on how far a crowd formed; neither provides a clear same-site estimate of at least 50.
threshold_50_evidence: Pending. RFE/RL reports several dozen at a rally, while DW describes a prevented assembly and only several people walking across the square; these accounts do not establish a same-site group of at least 50. Do not treat a detention count as turnout.

title.summary: RFE/RL and OVD-Info identify a Jan. 30 Furgal-support action; DW describes police preventing people from gathering in Lenin Square that day.

start_date.summary: Both the RFE/RL report date/event description and DW’s retrospective chronology identify Jan. 30, 2021.

end_date.summary: Neither report establishes a precise physical end. DW says other activists left after seeing no group assembled, while RFE/RL describes several dozen at a rally; the conflicting accounts do not establish full departure or a continuous episode end.

location.summary: The sources place the Furgal-support action at the central square/Lenin Square in Khabarovsk; the OVD-Info body itself was blocked, while RFE/RL and DW bodies were read.

scope.summary: RFE/RL describes several dozen attendees at a Furgal-support rally; DW says police prevented people from assembling and detained individuals walking around the square. The scope and crowd formation conflict remains unresolved.

organizer.summary: Neither read report identifies a named Jan. 30 organizer; the Furgal-support label is not a full organizer roster.

demands.summary: RFE/RL identifies the action as support for Furgal. It also says no posters or chants were observed; no more specific Jan. 30 demand is documented. Prior campaign demands are not transferred to this date.

participants_original.summary: RFE/RL says several dozen people attended; DW says police prevented a group from assembling and only several people walking across the square were detained, with other activists leaving. These conflicting descriptions do not yield a reliable numeric count.

threshold_50_evidence.summary: The accounts conflict on whether a gathering formed. “Several dozen” from RFE/RL does not clearly establish 50 or more, and DW does not describe a formed crowd. No attendance threshold is inferred from arrests.

protester_violence.summary: No event-specific assessment of participant violence is provided; no posters or chants is not evidence that violence was absent, so unknown.

state_response.accommodation.summary: Neither source documents reception or negotiation of a Jan. 30 demand; unknown.

state_response.arrests.summary: RFE/RL attributes several detentions to OVD-Info/eyewitnesses, including a journalist, three elderly people and people said to be passersby; DW independently reports several people walking across Lenin Square were detained. The attributed reports support arrests, not turnout.

state_response.beatings.summary: Neither article establishes state beatings during this Jan. 30 event; unknown.

state_response.crowd_dispersal.summary: DW reports police prevented people from gathering together on the square and detained people who walked there. This supports an attributed attempt to prevent assembly, not a claim that a formed crowd was successfully dispersed.

state_response.ignore.summary: No explicit state avoidance or refusal of a Jan. 30 request is documented. General Furgal-campaign history is not coded as this event’s ignore response.

state_response.killings.summary: Neither report identifies an event-related state killing; no explicit finding of absence is made, so unknown.

state_response.shootings.summary: Neither report establishes firearm discharge at the Jan. 30 action; unknown.

notes: The event date and Furgal-support framing are documented, but RFE/RL’s “several dozen” and DW’s report that police prevented people assembling conflict on crowd formation and do not establish >=50. RFE/RL says there were no posters or chants; that is not a no-violence finding. The detention reports support arrests, with attribution and possible passersby noted. Earlier Furgal campaign demands are not transferred to this date; a specific demand, physical boundary and episode ownership remain review questions.
open_questions: Did a public gathering of at least 50 form before police prevented assembly, or is the RFE/RL account inconsistent with DW’s observation?
What specific state-directed demand, if any, was articulated on Jan. 30?
Is this a new physical episode within the earlier weekly campaign or an older-onset continuation?
